name: Heavy Psych
about: Heavy psych is the loud end of the psychedelic rock of the late 1960s: fuzz and feedback turned up past the point where the blues could contain them, with drums that hit rather than swing and vocals shouted over the din. Hendrix was the model, Cream the respectable version, and Blue Cheer's Vincebus Eruptum in 1968 the moment the style became its own thing; Iron Butterfly, Vanilla Fudge, High Tide and Britain's Groundhogs followed, as did Japan's Flower Travellin' Band. It bled into proto-metal and then into metal proper, but the loose, jam-based, acid-dazed strain never died: Monster Magnet revived it in the 1990s, and Comets on Fire, Earthless and Acid Mothers Temple keep the extended freak-out alive today.

artists.name: Iron Butterfly
artists.why: took the drum solo to the charts

artists.name: Acid Mothers Temple & The Melting Paraiso U.F.O.

albums.title: Are You Experienced
albums.why: The debut that rewrote what an electric guitar could do, from 'Purple Haze' to 'Third Stone from the Sun'; the heaviest psychedelia of 1967 by a distance.

albums.title: Electric Ladyland
albums.why: A sprawling double album of studio experiment, blues and the fifteen-minute 'Voodoo Chile'; Hendrix's fullest statement and his last with the Experience.

albums.title: Disraeli Gears
albums.why: Clapton, Bruce and Baker at their most concise, with Felix Pappalardi's production giving 'Sunshine of Your Love' and 'Tales of Brave Ulysses' a lysergic sheen.

albums.title: Satori
albums.why: Joe Yamanaka's wail and Hideki Ishima's sitar-inflected riffs across five numbered movements; Japan's great contribution to heavy psychedelia and still startling.

albums.title: Vincebus Eruptum
albums.why: Three San Francisco bikers playing 'Summertime Blues' at punishing volume; crude, overdriven and arguably the first heavy metal record.

albums.title: Sea Shanties
albums.why: Tony Hill's guitar and Simon House's violin duelling over relentless riffs; a Liberty Records obscurity that heavy-psych collectors treat as a holy text.

albums.title: Split
albums.why: Tony McPhee's trio stretching the blues into a four-part suite about mental collapse on side one and pure boogie on side two; their best.

albums.title: Captain Beyond
albums.why: Ex-members of Deep Purple and Iron Butterfly stitching heavy riffs into odd-metred suites; a cult record that connects psych to early prog metal.

albums.title: Wheels of Fire
albums.why: A studio disc of lush psychedelic blues paired with a live one from the Fillmore; the extended 'Spoonful' and 'Crossroads' set the template for the heavy jam.

albums.title: In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida
albums.why: The seventeen-minute title track, drum solo and all, sold millions and defined the genre's excess; the rest of the record is slight.

albums.title: Vanilla Fudge
albums.why: Slowed-down, organ-heavy covers of the Supremes and the Beatles played as if they were cathedrals; ponderous, but a real influence on Deep Purple.

albums.title: Kingdom Come
albums.why: A Brooklyn trio so loud and distorted that a 1971 review reached for the phrase 'heavy metal' to describe them; raw and tuneless in the best way.

albums.title: Growers of Mushroom
albums.why: Peter French's blues shout over Mick Halls' fuzz on a record that sold nothing and became one of the most sought-after British heavy-psych LPs.

albums.title: Climbing!
albums.why: Leslie West's thick tone and Felix Pappalardi's bass on 'Mississippi Queen' and 'Theme for an Imaginary Western'; a bridge from Cream to American hard rock.

albums.title: Eve
albums.why: A Filipino drummer, a Japanese guitarist and a bassist from Osaka making sludgy, stoned heavy blues in Tokyo; a cult Japanese record that still sounds wild.

albums.title: Volcanic Rock
albums.why: Sydney's answer to Black Sabbath, with Dave Tice's bellow and a sleeve that got it banned; the heaviest Australian record of its era.

albums.title: Heavier Than a Death in the Family
albums.why: Mizutani's long-bootlegged Tokyo band on their most widely heard release, a live compilation where feedback swallows the songs whole; a monument of Japanese underground rock.

albums.title: Spine of God
albums.why: Dave Wyndorf's New Jersey band pulling Hawkwind and Blue Cheer into the 1990s with sludge, samples and a sense of humour; a cornerstone of the revival.

albums.title: Blue Cathedral
albums.why: Ethan Miller's Santa Cruz band at their most expansive, with Ben Chasny's guitar and echoplex noise fused into a genuinely new heavy psychedelia.

albums.title: Rhythms from a Cosmic Sky
albums.why: Two side-long instrumental jams from the San Diego trio, built on Mario Rubalcaba's drumming and Isaiah Mitchell's unending solos; the modern heavy-psych benchmark.

albums.title: Shivering King and Others
albums.why: The Washington, DC trio's third record, drenched in reverb and Sabbath fuzz, moving at a stoned, melodic crawl; their most consistent.

albums.artist: Acid Mothers Temple & The Melting Paraiso U.F.O.
albums.title: La Nòvia
albums.why: Kawabata Makoto's commune turning an Occitan folk tune into a side-long drone of acid guitar and chant; the gentlest entry point to a vast discography.

albums.title: Blood Lust
albums.why: Kevin Starrs' Cambridge trio recorded in lo-fi with Sabbath riffs and Beatles harmonies about a witch-hunter; a sleeper cult hit that revived the 1970s sound.

albums.title: Lore
albums.why: The Massachusetts band's third record stretches stoner riffing into long, melodic progressive pieces with real compositional ambition; one of the best heavy records of its decade.
